about: City heat ecosystem profiles for Delhi, Mumbai, Ahmedabad, Kolkata, Chennai, Hyderabad, Bhubaneswar, Dhaka and Kathmandu (/cities/<city>/who-is-doing-what/), November 2026. Each claim is tied to the exact words its source has to hold; stage.js stages the sources in data/inbox/2026-11-city-ecosystems/, verify-sources.yml checks them, and gate.js writes confirmed.json. Only confirmed claims reach the pages. Researched 28 November 2026 from public sources only; no organisation was contacted.

claims.text: In 2013 Ahmedabad became the first city in South Asia to launch its own Heat Action Plan, which includes an early warning system and awareness campaigns.
rests_on: first city in South Asia to launch its own Heat Action Plan

claims.text: An evaluation by researchers, cited by the WHO Foundation, found the plan helped save 1,190 lives every year in its first five years.
NRDC writes that after the 2010 heat wave, experts estimated that heat contributed to more than 1,000 deaths in the city.
rests_on: heat contributed to more than 1,000 deaths

claims.text: In 2017 the Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation piloted cool roofs on over 3,000 low-income homes as part of the Heat Action Plan, with NRDC, IIPH Gandhinagar and Mahila Housing Trust as partners, using white lime paint; NRDC gives a total programme cost of ₹700,000 for 2017.
rests_on: pilot cool roofs program for over 3,000 low income homes
Indian Institute of Public Health- Gandhinagar (IIPH-G) and Mahila Housing Trust (MHT)

claims.text: NRDC says the pilot was carried out by city staff, over 50 volunteer students and local civil society groups, and engaged 20 to 25 real estate developers to apply cool roofs to private buildings voluntarily in 2018.
In April 2019 NRDC reported the city was scaling up to a city-wide cool roof programme and meeting stakeholders on the draft.
rests_on: scaling up to a city-wide cool roof program

claims.text: Mahila Housing Trust runs a Cool Roofs Initiative within the city's Heat Action Plan, painting the roofs of low-income homes with heat-reflective paint; in June 2025 Down To Earth reported that the Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation had included cool roofs in the plan.
rests_on: Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation (AMC) has included this

claims.text: With the Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, Mahila Housing Trust installed a high-pressure misting system at the Lal Darwaza bus stop; Mahila Housing Trust says waiting passengers get at least 4 to 7°C of relief.

Mahila Housing Trust offers women in informal work a heat insurance launched in April 2024 that pays out automatically when temperatures cross set thresholds; in May 2024 a threshold was crossed and payouts followed.
rests_on: In May 2024, the lower threshold was breached

claims.text: Down To Earth (June 2025) describes two thresholds, 43.7°C and 44.1°C, paying Rs 750 and a further Rs 1,250, up to Rs 2,000 a year for an annual premium of Rs 354.
The WHO Foundation (September 2024) describes one trigger of 44.2 ºC and up to 2,000 rupees a season.
Scroll reported in March 2025 that Ahmedabad keeps its 293 parks open from 6 am to 11 pm for shade, has put up 120 heatstroke signboards and holds weekly meetings of all departments on the plan.
rests_on: 293 parks open from 6 am till 11 pm

claims.text: The Government of Delhi launched the Delhi Heat Action Plan 2025 on 21 April 2025, with a city-wide early warning system developed with the IMD to issue graded alerts and special air-conditioned units in hospitals for heatstroke.
rests_on: early warning system developed with IMD

claims.text: The plan promised nearly 3,000 water coolers, cooling shelters on roads, shaded footpaths and green roofs, and the recruitment of Aapda Mitra disaster volunteers.
ThePrint reported that the Delhi government was working with the IMD and the NDMA on the plan.
The plan floated cool roof pilots at the Delhi Secretariat, Kashmere Gate ISBT and Anand Vihar ISBT.
rests_on: Delhi Secretariat, Kashmere Gate ISBT and Anand Vihar ISBT

claims.text: The plan includes a pilot of white roof painting, or gunny bags for tin and asbestos roofs, in slums; a housing rights worker told Newslaundry in April 2025 that no such action had been implemented as far as they knew.
rests_on: pilot project on roof painting with white colour
No such actions as far as I know have been implemented

claims.text: The plan asks the Delhi Transport Corporation to provide bus shelters with drinking water; a union leader told Newslaundry none of the measures were in action.
rests_on: None of the measures mentioned are in action

claims.text: Newslaundry reported that heat is not among the notified disasters, so Delhi cannot draw on its State Disaster Response Fund for heat, although that fund rose from Rs 300 lakh in 2024-25 to Rs 2,500 lakh in 2025-26.
A Centre for Science and Environment analysis found almost 76 per cent of Delhi facing heat stress in summer months over 2015 to 2024, and rated Matiala the only ward of very high vulnerability.

A two-round survey by WIEGO found 90 per cent of Delhi street vendors cut their working hours in the 2025 heatwave; none of 17 major markets mapped had a municipal water point, and fewer than one-third of vendors received timely heat alerts.
rests_on: none of the markets had a municipal water point
Less than one-third of vendors reported receiving timely heat alerts

claims.text: The same survey found some women vendors had better support through organisations such as SEWA, and that borrowing among vendors doubled between the two rounds.

Greenpeace India and the National Hawkers Federation surveyed over 700 Delhi street vendors; 49.27% reported lost income during heatwaves, and the report urged the Delhi Heat Action Plan authority to consult vendors and other outdoor workers.
rests_on: consult with vendors and other outdoor workers

claims.text: A study of 396 workers in two Delhi informal settlements found their earnings were 40% lower on the hottest days.
rests_on: 396 workers living in two informal settlements in Delhi

claims.text: Mahila Housing Trust, with the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago and the University of Chicago Energy and Environment Lab, has studied whether heat-reflective roof paint lowers indoor temperatures in Delhi.
rests_on: Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago (EPIC-India)

claims.text: IGSSS fitted thirty Delhi houses with wall panels in a pilot run between April 2022 and March 2023.
rests_on: Thirty houses were fitted with the panels on the walls

claims.text: The Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation launched the Mumbai Climate Action Plan in 2022; drafted by the World Resources Institute, it treats heatwaves under urban heat.
rests_on: Drafted by the World Resources Institute

claims.text: Citizen Matters reported in August 2024 that little had moved on the plan since the change in power.
rests_on: little has moved since the change in power

claims.text: The corporation set up a Climate Action Cell with WRI India; in June 2025 only four of its 41 sanctioned positions were filled.
rests_on: Climate Action Cell with WRI India
only four out of total 41 sanctioned positions

claims.text: The corporation's second climate budget was Rs 17,000 crores, 37% of its capital expenditure, and it reported 86.26% financial progress on its 2024-25 climate budget.
Informal settlements in Mumbai show land surface temperatures 5 to 8 degrees higher than neighbouring areas.

The corporation, supported by C40 Cities and Tarutium Global Consulting, developed an implementation pathway on heat targeting building-sector hotspots, using baseline assessments and ground-truthing in three areas; it covers reflective materials and nature-based solutions and outlines protections for construction workers.
rests_on: BMC, supported by C40 Cities and Tarutium Global Consulting, developed an implementation pathway

claims.text: Scroll reported in March 2025 that the city's 1,000-plus parks, gardens and playgrounds stay shut in the afternoon, open 5 am to 1 pm and 3 pm to 10 pm.
rests_on: 5 am to 1 pm and 3 pm to 10 pm

claims.text: A volunteer group, the Heatwave action coalition, and cBalance, which designs low-cost ways to cool homes in slums, were named by Citizen Matters in August 2024.
rests_on: Heatwave action coalition is a group of volunteers
low cost innovations that lower the temperature in the houses in slums

claims.text: A cool roof programme for schools is being expanded to 55 schools in Chennai, 49 Corporation schools and six government schools, implemented through the TN Green Climate Company with UNEP under the TN Climate Change Mission; work was already complete in five government schools in June 2026.
rests_on: 49 Corporation schools and six government schools
Work has already been completed in five government schools

claims.text: The Greater Chennai Corporation trained teachers and headmasters for the programme, which targets schools in areas vulnerable to high temperatures.
rests_on: training programme for teachers and headmasters

claims.text: The Greater Chennai Corporation and CEEW signed a memorandum of understanding on extreme heat risk management in July 2026; a Project Management Unit is to prioritise heat mitigation in heat-vulnerable wards and zones and prepare Detailed Project Reports.
rests_on: Project Management Unit (PMU) will be established

claims.text: UNEP's Cool Coalition and CEPT University mapped the city's heat; their recommendations, projected to reduce urban heat by up to 4°C, are being integrated into the master plan.
rests_on: These recommendations are being integrated into

claims.text: That work was supported by the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation, the Government of Denmark, the Clean Cooling Collaborative and the World Bank.
rests_on: Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation

claims.text: Tamil Nadu's government has declared heat a disaster.

In 2017 the Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation, with ASCI, IIIT-H and NRDC, ran a cool roofs pilot on 25 city roofs in one low-income neighbourhood; indoor air was on average 2°C cooler and 76% of residents in the trial group were satisfied.
rests_on: partnered with ASCI, IIIT-H, and NRDC
25 city roofs in one low-income neighborhood

claims.text: The Telangana Cool Roofs Policy 2023-2028 aims to convert roofs across 300 square kilometres of the state, 200 of them in Hyderabad, by 2028-29, starting with 5 sq km of Hyderabad in 2023-2024.
rests_on: 200 sq km will be in Hyderabad
5 sq km area of Hyderabad in 2023-2024

claims.text: NRDC wrote that the policy took effect on 1 April 2023, is built into building permit applications, makes cool roofs mandatory in government low-cost housing, and is to reach low-income homes through city Heat Action Plans.
NRDC gives the residential threshold as a plot area of 600 sq. m and above.
ThePrint gives it as properties over 600 square yards.
The policy is led by Telangana's Municipal Administration and Urban Development Department; NRDC wrote that it and ASCI, IIIT-H and Plaksha University would work with the state on it.
In 2019 IIIT Hyderabad was testing 20 samples of roof materials on rooftop racks over five years across four cities.

Telangana released its Heatwave Action Plan 2025 on 2 May 2025, prepared by the Revenue (Disaster Management) Department with inputs from the IMD and UNICEF's Hyderabad field office; declaring heat a state disaster lets Telangana use 10% of its State Disaster Response Fund on heatwaves.
rests_on: released its Heatwave Action Plan (HAP) for 2025 on May 2
10% of the State Disaster Response Funds

claims.text: The News Minute reported that Hyderabad's relief measures start once temperatures cross 40°C, when the Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation and other departments act under the plan, and that the measures are directory, without legal backing.

For summer 2026 the Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation put in place a preparedness and mitigation plan: drinking water kiosks (chalivendrams), coordination with urban health centres and Basti Dawakhanas, medical camps at construction sites, and IMD heat warnings on digital boards at major junctions.
rests_on: medical camps have been organised at construction sites
digital boards at major traffic junctions

claims.text: In September 2025 the Bhubaneswar Municipal Corporation launched the city's first Integrated Heat and Cooling Action Plan, developed by iFOREST with the Singapore-ETH Centre.
rests_on: first Integrated Heat and Cooling Action Plan (IHCAP)
International Forum for Environment, Sustainability and Technology (iFOREST)

claims.text: The plan projects that the city could face a sevenfold rise in cooling electricity demand by 2050.
rests_on: sevenfold rise in cooling electricity demand by 2050

claims.text: It calls for urban greening in all wards toward the WHO benchmark of nine square metres per person, and strict implementation of the Odisha Energy Conservation Building Codes.
rests_on: expansion of urban greening in all wards

claims.text: Between 2018 and 2024 built-up areas in the city grew by 23 per cent and water bodies shrank by 75 per cent, according to the plan's findings as reported.
rests_on: built-up areas in the capital grew by 23 per cent
water bodies shrank by an alarming 75 per cent

claims.text: If implemented, the plan's measures are projected to lower surface temperatures by 0.5 to 9.4 degrees Celsius; this is a modelled projection of surface temperature, not air temperature.
An earlier Climate Adaptive Heat Action Plan for Bhubaneswar was prepared by IRADe.
A Centre for Science and Environment assessment of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation area found very severe and severe heat zones covering 11.82 per cent and 38.25 per cent of the municipal area.
A 2022-23 study by the Centre for Science and Environment showed the city's water bodies decreased by 39 per cent and its vegetation by 19 per cent.
rests_on: water bodies decreased by 39 per cent

claims.text: Scientists quoted by Down To Earth in May 2024 said the city needs a heat action plan.
rests_on: it definitely needs a heat action plan

claims.text: West Bengal has a state Heat Wave Action Plan prepared by its disaster management department.
A study of nine high-risk cities, including Kolkata, found 150 heat-related measures between 2018 and 2023, most of them seasonal or taken after heatwaves had struck.
rests_on: Nine-high risk cities, including New Delhi, Bhopal, Kolkata and Varanasi

claims.text: In May 2023 Dhaka North City Corporation appointed a Chief Heat Officer under a joint initiative with Arsht-Rock, the first of its kind in Asia, with Shakti Foundation as a local partner.
rests_on: first of its kind in Asia

claims.text: Arsht-Rock and UN-Habitat collaborate to support a global Chief Heat Officer.
By July 2023 the city authority had set up 100 water booths; the Chief Heat Officer planned cooling zones with water, ventilation and shaded seating.
Dhaka North announced plans to plant trees and create parks and approved a tax incentive for rooftop gardens.
rests_on: tax incentive for those who set up gardens on their rooftops

claims.text: ICLEI was preparing climate change action plans for Dhaka's two city corporations in 2023.
The Bangladesh Red Crescent Society, with the German and Danish Red Cross, was working with urban working-class people and planned healthcare and cash grants for vulnerable families.
rests_on: Bangladesh Red Crescent Society together with the German and Danish Red Cross

claims.text: On 21 April 2024 the Bangladesh Red Crescent Society activated its Early Action Protocol for heatwaves in Dhaka for the first time, funded by the IFRC's Disaster Response Emergency Fund with 499,930 Swiss francs.
rests_on: for the first time activated its early action protocol for heatwave

claims.text: The planned actions were multipurpose cash grants for the most vulnerable, such as elderly people and outdoor workers, cooling stations in three strategic locations, ambulance support, early warning messages and safe drinking water, focused on Adabor, Gendaria, Kamrangir Char, Lalbagh, Mohammadpur and Pallabi.
rests_on: cooling stations in three strategic locations
Adabor, Gendaria, Kamrangir Char, Lalbagh, Mohammadpur and Pallabi

claims.text: The Anticipation Hub gives the target as 123,700 vulnerable people.
The Climate Centre gives it as 124,000 vulnerable people.

Under the Department of Environment, the Institute of Water Modelling collected a year of microclimate data from more than 20 points across the capital from April 2024; findings are to inform a proposed Heat Action Plan.
rests_on: more than 20 points across the capital

claims.text: Kathmandu recorded 35.3 degrees Celsius in June 2024, its highest temperature on record.
rests_on: 35.3 degrees Celsius in Kathmandu in June 2024

claims.text: Researchers writing in 2023 found no comprehensive heat plan in Nepal, and that heat illness and excess deaths are not systematically tracked.
In June 2025 UN-Habitat Nepal staff called for a robust early warning system and preparedness, and noted permeable pavements tested in Lalitpur Metropolitan.
rests_on: permeable pavements tested in Lalitpur Metropolitan

claims.text: The Annapurna Express reported in 2024 that urban green spaces, tree planting and community-managed forests are underway, while public awareness of urban heat lags.
rests_on: Urban Green Spaces (UGS), tree plantations and community-managed forests are underway

claims.text: A 2026 study, Hot Cities Make Hard Work Harder, co-published by People's Courage International, surveyed 305 migrant workers in Kathmandu; 46 percent reported being negatively affected.
rests_on: Hot Cities Make Hard Work Harder

claims.text: A 2026 World Bank report, A Livable Future, found the city core up to 4 degrees Celsius hotter than surrounding parts of the valley and recommended retrofitting heritage sites in the Kathmandu Valley.
rests_on: retrofitting heritage sites in the Kathmandu Valley
